patterns.name: Consonant gradation
patterns.summary: Closed syllables weaken stem consonants (kk→k, pp→p, tt→t, and more).
patterns.description: Finnish noun and verb stems often alternate between a strong and a weak grade. When a suffix creates a closed syllable (ending in a consonant), many stops weaken: kukka → kukan, matto → maton, puku → puvun. Learning the common pairs is essential before productive case and tense morphology.
patterns.source_note: Wikibooks: Suomen kieli ulkomaalaisille / Finnish Language for Foreigners (CC BY-SA; cited by topic, not reproduced), consonant gradation / astevaihtelu

examples.prompt: kukka in the genitive is kukan. Which change is that?
examples.note: Quantitative gradation: long stop shortens in a closed syllable.

examples.prompt: What happens to tt in matto → maton?
examples.note: Same quantitative pattern as kk→k and pp→p.

examples.prompt: puku → puvun shows which qualitative change?
examples.note: Single k between vowels often becomes v in the weak grade.

examples.prompt: tieto → tiedon: the weak grade of t here is…
examples.note: t ~ d is a frequent qualitative pair.

patterns.name: Verb rections
patterns.summary: Many verbs require a specific case or adposition on their complement.
patterns.description: Finnish verbs often select the case of their object or complement (rection). pitää + -sta means ‘like’; tutustua takes the illative; odottaa takes the partitive. Memorising frames with the verb prevents calquing English prepositions incorrectly.
patterns.source_note: Wikibooks: Suomen kieli ulkomaalaisille / Finnish Language for Foreigners (CC BY-SA; cited by topic, not reproduced), verb rections / verbien rektiot

examples.prompt: With pitää ‘like’, the liked thing usually takes which case?
examples.note: pitää + elative = ‘to like’.

examples.prompt: tutustua ‘get to know’ typically takes…
examples.note: The person/thing becomes the destination of ‘getting acquainted’.

examples.gloss_en: I am waiting for the bus.
examples.prompt: odottaa ‘wait for’ takes which object case in this progressive sense?
examples.note: Waiting is unbounded; the object is partitive.

examples.prompt: kuulua ‘belong’ often takes…
examples.note: Belonging is framed as ‘into’ a set.

patterns.name: Partitive vs accusative (object case)
patterns.summary: Resultative completed objects take -n; incomplete or unbounded ones take partitive.
patterns.description: Finnish object case encodes aspect and boundedness. A completed, resultative action with a countable whole often uses the accusative/genitive -n (Luin kirjan). Ongoing, partial, negated, or mass/indefinite objects use the partitive (Luen kirjaa; En lukenut kirjaa). This opposition is central to Finnish and has no English preposition equivalent.
patterns.source_note: Wikibooks: Suomen kieli ulkomaalaisille / Finnish Language for Foreigners (CC BY-SA; cited by topic, not reproduced), partitive and total object

examples.prompt: Luin kirjan implies the reading was…
examples.note: -n marks a bounded completed object.

examples.gloss_en: I am reading a/the book (not finished).
examples.prompt: Luen kirjaa uses the partitive because the event is…
examples.note: Partitive object with present progressive reading.

examples.prompt: Mass nouns as objects are typically…
examples.note: Water is unbounded stuff → partitive.

examples.prompt: A single countable purchase often takes…
examples.note: Contrast: Ostin omenaa could mean ‘some apple (substance)’.

patterns.name: Locative cases (internal and external)
patterns.summary: Internal: -ssa/-sta/-Vn; external: -lla/-lta/-lle for place and many abstract uses.
patterns.description: Finnish has two parallel place-case series. Internal cases (inessive -ssa, elative -sta, illative -Vn) treat the landmark as a container. External cases (adessive -lla, ablative -lta, allative -lle) treat it as a surface or vicinity. The same endings also mark time, possession (minulla on…), instruments, and more.
patterns.source_note: Wikibooks: Suomen kieli ulkomaalaisille / Finnish Language for Foreigners (CC BY-SA; cited by topic, not reproduced), local cases / sijamuodot

examples.gloss_en: in the house / out of the house / into the house
examples.prompt: Which series is talossa–talosta–taloon?
examples.note: Inessive, elative, illative.

examples.gloss_en: on the table / off the table / onto the table
examples.prompt: pöydällä–pöydältä–pöydälle belong to which series?
examples.note: Adessive, ablative, allative.

examples.prompt: Possession ‘I have’ is typically expressed with…
examples.note: External adessive marks the possessor.

examples.prompt: Time expressions like kesällä use which ending family?
examples.note: Locatives extend beyond physical space.

patterns.name: Vowel harmony
patterns.summary: Suffix vowels match the stem: back a/o/u vs front ä/ö/y; e/i are neutral.
patterns.description: Finnish suffixes alternate for vowel harmony. Stems with back vowels (a, o, u) take back endings (-ssa, -lla); stems with front vowels (ä, ö, y) take front endings (-ssä, -llä). Neutral e and i do not force a series by themselves.
patterns.source_note: Wikibooks: Suomen kieli ulkomaalaisille / Finnish Language for Foreigners (CC BY-SA; cited by topic, not reproduced), vowel harmony / vokaaliharmonia

examples.gloss_en: in the house / in the forest
examples.prompt: Why metsässä and not *metsassa?
examples.note: metsä has ä → front inessive -ssä.

examples.prompt: pöytä takes -llä rather than -lla because…
examples.note: Front stem → front adessive.

examples.prompt: Helsinki ends in neutral i but uses -ssä. Why?
examples.answer: earlier syllables contain front/e-quality; learned with the name
examples.note: Place names must be learned with their harmony class.

patterns.name: Negation and object case
patterns.summary: ei conjugates for person; objects under negation are typically partitive.
patterns.description: Negation uses the defective verb ei plus a connegative form of the main verb (en lue, et lue, ei lue). Objects in negative clauses almost always appear in the partitive (En lukenut kirjaa), even when the affirmative would take -n.
patterns.source_note: Wikibooks: Suomen kieli ulkomaalaisille / Finnish Language for Foreigners (CC BY-SA; cited by topic, not reproduced), negation / kielto

examples.gloss_en: I am not reading / do not read the book.
examples.prompt: Under negation, the object kirja appears as…
examples.note: Negative clauses prefer partitive objects.

examples.prompt: In the past negative, the main verb is…
examples.note: ei + participle builds past negation.

examples.prompt: The negative imperative for ‘you (sg)’ uses…
examples.note: älä / älkää are the prohibitive forms.
